newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: FEATURE - Singapore WTO preparations no laughing matter.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Singapore WTO preparations no laughing matter.

text.p: "Kiasu", a word frequently used in Singapore and literally meaning "scared to lose," could describe the meticulous preparations for the World Trade Organisation (WTO) Ministerial Conference.

"We cannot afford to fail because Singapore's name and reputation depends on us," Goh Chee Wee, Minister of State for Trade and Industry and Communications, told a group of about 250 front-line staff recently.

More than 6,000 people in the city-state are being mobilised to look after the needs of about 4,000 delegates and around 1,000 foreign journalists expected to arrive for the conference, which runs between December 9 and 13.
SERVICE WITH A SMILE

While the hardware can be counted on to run like clockwork, as millions are spent to keep the infrastructure ticking with Singapore's well-known efficiency, the government is taking seriously the prospect that the Singaporeans the delegates encounter may not produce that "million dollar smile."
"To all service providers please remember always to be courteous, helpful and to serve with a smile", Goh said.

Singaporeans have a reputation in Southeast Asia for ungracious behaviour stemming from the "Kiasu" mentality and this has led to calls, even by the Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong, for them to be more civil.
As a result of the Prime Minister's comments, a "Small Kindness Movement" was started in September to get Singaporeans to make random acts of kindness second nature.

The movement supplements the state's annual "Courtesy Campaign" which is in its 17th year, and is in addition to the recently launched "Smile, Singapore" campaign to persuade locals to smile at tourists.

But just in case the odd visitor bumps into an ungracious Singaporean, the organisers are hoping that this experience will be forgotton when the visitor samples the country's renowned and culturally diverse cuisine.
Singapore is going to great lengths to prepare the country's best meals for the delegates and is drawing on its inheritance of Chinese, Malaysian and Indian dishes.
Lavish receptions and a grand farewell dinner at a resort island are planned for delegates so they can savour the local tropical delights.
FREE LUNCH
Visiting journalists are being offered free buffet meals ranging from the local delicacies to cuisine from Brazil, Thailand and Italy.

Armed with a Singapore $18 million (U.S.$12.8 million) budget, the city-state is even replacing each of the more than 1,000 light bulbs that adorn the Singapore International Convention & Exhibition Centre.

A fleet of 200 new BMW 728i cars will be driven by hand-picked taxi drivers to chauffeur the heads of delegations. The cars provided free by a local BMW agent will subsequently be sold at a nine percent discount at S$255,000 each.

Delegates will also receive a souvenir pack that includes a special card for free travel on local public transport, a CD featuring the Singapore Symphony Orchestra and even a S$10 prepaid phone card for international calls home.

An extensive social programme for people accompanying the delegates has been mapped and will take them to all the island's main tourist spots such as the Night Safari Zoo, the Singapore Zoo and the Orchid Garden.
If all the local sights on the tiny island are exhausted, tours outside Singapore have also been arranged to the neighbouring Indonesian Bintan and Batam islands.
-- Singapore Newsroom (+65-870-3093)
